missionCards.name: Wildfire Watch
missionCards.objective: Detect wildfires early from space over a target region.
missionCards.whyItMatters: Early detection gives firefighters hours instead of days. A satellite can watch remote forests that no lookout tower or patrol covers.
missionCards.destination: Low Earth orbit (LEO). You choose the orbit type and altitude.

requirements.title: Daily revisit
requirements.text: See the target region at least once per day.
requirements.failText: The satellite does not pass over the region every day. Pick a wider-angle instrument or a higher orbit so each pass covers a wider strip.

requirements.title: Daylight fire detection
requirements.text: Carry an instrument able to detect active fires in daylight.
requirements.failText: None of the chosen instruments can spot an active fire. A shortwave or thermal infrared instrument can, because fires are very bright at those wavelengths.

requirements.title: Enough data on the ground
requirements.text: Downlink at least 1 GB of data per day.
requirements.failText: Too little data reaches the ground each day. Add a ground station for more contact time, or a faster radio.

requirements.title: One year in orbit
requirements.failText: The orbit decays too fast and the satellite re-enters the atmosphere too early. Fly higher, or carry propulsion to raise the orbit.

bonusObjectives.name: Night detection
bonusObjectives.text: Carry a thermal infrared instrument, so fires are also seen at night.

bonusObjectives.name: Twice-daily revisit
bonusObjectives.text: See the region at least twice per day.

bonusObjectives.name: Fast alerts
bonusObjectives.text: Deliver data to the ground within 1 hour of an observation. This needs more ground station contacts.

tradeOffs: Power vs data: a better camera needs more power and produces more data, but ground contact time is short.
Revisit vs sharpness: with one satellite, a daily revisit needs a wide swath (a wide-angle instrument or a higher orbit), and both give less sharp images.
Altitude: a lower orbit gives sharper images but decays sooner.
Orbit type: a sun-synchronous orbit passes at the same local time every day; other orbits may revisit the region more often.
Launch choice: a rideshare is cheap but its orbit is fixed; a dedicated small launcher lets you choose the orbit but takes a large share of the budget.
Technology vs time: advanced parts improve performance but risk missing the fire-season deadline.

sources.note: Starting values for balancing; not real-world figures.
A fire-prone region at mid-latitude, so orbit type matters for revisit and ground contact.
